queries.hook: Being asked to choose between the life your parents have pictured and the life you have actually built, and the anger of feeling you will lose a part of yourself either way.
queries.diagnose: When others see only a role, their picture is their smallness and not your measure; the harm deepens only when their picture begins to replace your own.
queries.steady: What you are cannot be cut smaller by what they see; your worth was never theirs to grant, and standing in your own truth is itself the duty.
queries.act: Speak the true thing gently and firmly, hold your ground on what is yours, and do your own duty without shrinking to fit the picture they hold.
queries.story: A woman who was asked to choose between two worlds, who questioned her own people and stood in her truth, and found her footing on the other side.

verse.speaker: Narrator
verse.setting: Kausalya hears her son must go into exile and is torn between duty and love.
verse.sanskrit: धरम सनेह उभयँ मति घेरी। भइ गति साँप छुछुंदरि केरी॥ राखउँ सुतहि करउँ अनुरोधू। धरमु जाइ अरु बंधु बिरोधू ॥
verse.line: Caught between duty and love, like a snake that can neither swallow nor let go.
verse.translation: Duty and love together hemmed in her mind; she was like the snake that has seized a muskrat. 'If I insist and keep my son, duty is lost and the brothers fall out...'
verse.why: Letting a child go with your blessing is love at its hardest.

prasang.title: Kausalya lets her son go
prasang.summary: Ram comes to his mother as she is preparing for his coronation. Torn between duty and love, she decides not to hold him back with 'false affection', blesses him and asks only that he not forget her. As he leaves she wonders aloud whether she will live to see his face again.
prasang.story_hook: She had the sweets ready for his coronation when he came to say goodbye.
prasang.lesson: Letting a child go with your blessing is love at its hardest.

verse.meaning: Kausalya stands in her chambers as the news arrives. She must send her son Ram into the forest. Her mind is caught between the duty she owes the kingdom and the love she owes her child. She is like a snake that has seized a muskrat. It cannot swallow, and it cannot let go. She knows that if she insists on keeping her son, duty is lost and the brothers fall out. She must let him go with her blessing. She has to choose the harder love, the love that sets free.
verse.for_you: You are caught between duty and love. You feel like a snake that cannot swallow its prey and cannot let it go. Your parents want you to choose their picture of you. They are asking you to hold on to something that is already gone.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse.sanskrit: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः ॥
verse.line: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.
verse.translation: Better is one's own duty, even done imperfectly, than the duty of another well done. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is full of fear.
verse.why: Your own path, imperfectly walked, beats a borrowed one.
verse.misuse: Not 'stay in the role your family or birth assigned you'. It's about being true to your own nature and calling.

prasang.title: The ignorant and the wise; act free of like and dislike
prasang.summary: Krishna contrasts the attached and the wise, warns that ego claims credit for what nature does, and says to follow your own path rather than imitate another's.
prasang.lesson: Your own path, imperfectly walked, beats a borrowed one.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is frozen, caught between his love for his family and his duty as a warrior. Krishna tells him that it is better to follow your own path, even if you stumble on it, than to wear a life that was never meant for you. A borrowed life, even a perfect one, is full of fear because it is not rooted in who you actually are.
verse.for_you: Your parents want you to wear a life that was never made for you. It feels like choosing them or losing a part of yourself, but both paths lead to a smaller life. Today, see that the fight is not about the boy.

verse.speaker: Ram
verse.setting: Ram has lain on the shore for three days asking the ocean for a way across. No answer comes.
verse.sanskrit: अवलेपः समुद्रस्य न दर्शयति यः स्वयम्। प्रशमश्च क्षमा चैव आर्जवं प्रियवादिता॥ असामर्थ्यफला ह्येते निर्गुणेषु सतां गुणाः।
verse.line: Calm, patience, honesty and kind words: people who don't value them will read them as weakness.
verse.translation: See the ocean's arrogance: he does not even show himself. Calm, forbearance, straightforwardness and gentle speech, these virtues of the good, are taken by the unworthy as signs of weakness.
verse.why: Be humble first. When humility is taken for weakness, act firmly, and stop once you're heard.
verse.misuse: Firmness only after real patience, and only toward someone who keeps ignoring you. When the ocean finally came, Ram listened and redirected the arrow.

prasang.title: Ram at the ocean: humble first, firm after
prasang.summary: Ram lies on kusha grass by the shore for three days, asking the ocean for a way. Ignored, he tells Lakshman that patience is being taken for weakness and takes up his bow. The ocean rises, offers a way (Nala's bridge), and Ram releases the arrow elsewhere at its request.
prasang.story_hook: For three days the prince lay on a bed of grass at the edge of the sea, asking politely.
prasang.lesson: Be humble first. When humility is taken for weakness, act firmly, and stop once you're heard.

verse.meaning: Ram lies on the shore for three days, asking the ocean for a way across. No answer comes. He tells Lakshman that patience is being taken for weakness. He takes up his bow and shoots. The ocean rises. Ram listens when it speaks, and redirects his arrow. The text says that calm, patience, honesty and kind words are read by the unworthy as weakness. It proposes that you be humble first. When humility is taken for weakness, act firmly, and stop once you're heard.
verse.for_you: What you are cannot be cut smaller by what they see; your worth was never theirs to grant, and standing in your own truth is itself the duty.

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: माऽऽत्मानमवमन्यस्व मैनमल्पेन बीभरः / मनः कृत्वा सुकल्याणं मा भैस्त्वं प्रतिसंहर
verse.line: Don't think less of yourself or settle for little. Set your mind on something good, and stop fearing.
verse.translation: Do not hold yourself in contempt, and do not keep it going on too little. Set your mind on what is truly good; don't be afraid. Pull yourself together.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.meaning: Queen Vidula finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She tells him not to hold himself in contempt or keep it going on too little. She tells him to set his mind on what is truly good and to stop being afraid. The point is that past failure does not define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.
verse.for_you: You are not failing by wanting a life that fits you. Your parents are afraid of a different future. Do not think less of yourself. Set your mind on what is truly good for you and stop fearing their disappointment.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on three kinds of food, effort, speech and giving.
verse.sanskrit: अनुद्वेगकरं वाक्यं सत्यं प्रियहितं च यत् । स्वाध्यायाभ्यसनं चैव वाङ्मयं तप उच्यते ॥
verse.line: Speak words that don't wound, that are true, kind and helpful. That is discipline of speech.
verse.translation: Speech that causes no distress, that is truthful, pleasant and beneficial, and the regular study of sacred texts: this is called austerity of speech.
verse.why: Speak kindly and truly, give without strings, and drop the show.
verse.misuse: Kind speech doesn't mean avoiding hard truths; it means saying them without cruelty.

prasang.title: Three kinds of food, offering, austerity and giving
prasang.summary: Food, offering, austerity and giving each come in three kinds. Speech should be true, kind and helpful; giving should expect nothing back; effort for show doesn't last.
prasang.lesson: Speak kindly and truly, give without strings, and drop the show.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna about the discipline of speech. He says that the best words are those that do not cause pain, that are true and kind, and that help. This is the austerity of speech. The idea is to speak without cruelty. It is not about hiding hard truths. It is about saying what is needed without wounding. The truth underneath is that your words can be both honest and gentle, and that is a strength.
verse.for_you: When your parents ask you to choose, try to speak the truth of what you feel without attacking them. You do not have to be cruel to be honest. Find the words that are true and kind, and let that be your discipline today.

verse.speaker: Brihaspati (retold by Bhishma)
verse.setting: Brihaspati counsels Indra on how to hold authority among difficult people.
verse.sanskrit: मृदुमप्यवमन्यन्ते तीक्ष्णादुद्विजते जनः / मातीक्ष्णो मा मृदुर्भूस्त्वं तीक्ष्णो भव मृदुर्भव
verse.line: People walk over the soft and fear the harsh. Be firm when it's needed, gentle when it's needed.
verse.translation: People look down even on the gentle, and they shrink from the harsh. Do not be only harsh, do not be only soft: be firm when firmness is needed and gentle when gentleness is.
verse.misuse: Firmness here means clarity, not cruelty.

verse.meaning: Brihaspati advises Indra that people look down on the gentle and shrink from the harsh. They tell him not to be only harsh, not to be only soft, but to be firm when firmness is needed and gentle when gentleness is. It says that people walk over the soft and fear the harsh, so balance is the strength that holds a room.
verse.for_you: When you set a boundary with your parents, be firm in what you need, but gentle in how you say it. You do not have to choose between being soft and being hard. You can be both, and that is a strength.

story.title: Parvati holds to her choice
story.story_hook: The sages came to talk Parvati out of it, and they listed every flaw in the man she had chosen.
story.summary: Reborn as Parvati, Sati resolves to marry Shiva and spends years in austerity. The seven sages come to test her, mocking Shiva as a homeless ascetic and offering her a better match. She answers that gold keeps its nature even in fire, and that the heart wants the one it has chosen.
story.lesson: Persistence is choosing the same thing again each day, even when others call it foolish.

anchor.speaker: Parvati
anchor.setting: Parvati answers the sages who mock her resolve to win Shiva through years of austerity.
anchor.sanskrit: सत्य कहेहु गिरिभव तनु एहा। हठ न छूट छूटै बरु देहा॥ कनकउ पुनि पषान तें होई। जारेहुँ सहजु न परिहर सोई ॥
anchor.line: Gold comes from stone, and even in fire it stays gold. Hold to what you are.
anchor.translation: You speak truly: this body was born of a mountain, so its resolve will not break, even if the body does. Gold too is born of stone, and even in fire it does not give up its nature.
anchor.why: Persistence is choosing the same thing again each day, even when others call it foolish.
anchor.misuse: Steadiness is not stubbornness; keep checking that the goal is still worth it.

script: You are torn right now. You are fighting with your parents and it feels like you are losing a part of yourself. You are caught between the life they want for you and the life you are living.
Kausalya hears her son must go into exile and is torn between duty and love. Narrator said to the reader:
धरम सनेह उभयँ मति घेरी, भइ गति साँप छुछुंदरि केरी. राखउँ सुतहि करउँ अनुरोधू, धरमु जाइ अरु बंधु बिरोधू.
In plain words: Caught between duty and love, like a snake that can neither swallow nor let go.

This is the hardest kind of love. It is the love that sets free. Kausalya knows that if she insists on keeping her son, duty is lost and the brothers fall out. She chooses to let him go with her blessing. This is easier said than done, because letting go feels like losing everything. But choosing your own life is not destroying theirs.

Your parents want you to hold on to a picture of you that is not real. You do not have to swallow their expectations, and you do not have to let go of who you are becoming. You can choose the harder love, the love that sets you free.
What part of you are you willing to let go of today?

depth.life: You are sitting with your phone in your hand, scrolling, and your chest is tight. You are fighting with your parents and you feel yourself being pulled in two directions. You are losing a part of yourself right now, and it hurts to feel split between the person you are becoming and the picture your family wants you to fit.
depth.points: The text shows a mother caught between duty and love. She cannot hold on without breaking the world, and she cannot let go without breaking her heart. You are living inside this same trap. Your parents are asking you to hold on to a picture that is not yours. Their smallness is what is holding you, not your worth.
depth.practice: Put your phone down for ten minutes. Sit with your hands still. Notice the pull in your chest without trying to fix it.
depth.question: What part of you are you most afraid they will not see?
